To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
APEC strains of the same phylogenetic subclusters as human ExPEC strains were highly virulent and expressed a similar set of virulence factors.
APEC strains of avian serotypes O1, O18, O2, or O78 are phylogenetically related to human ExPEC strains and that APEC strains are highly virulent for chickens.
APEC strains of human and animal origins are closely related and that the APEC strains of the serogroups O18, O1, and O2 are closely related to human strains of neonatal meningitidis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the virulence of APEC strains of human and chicken origin, and the phylogenetic relationship between these strains.
the genetic and virulence similarities between human ExPEC strains and APEC strains of the same phylogenetic group.
the phylogenetic and virulence relationships between avian APEC strains and ExPEC strains of human origin.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the APEC strains of the B2-1 phylogenetic group are highly pathogenic for chickens but also for humans.
APEC strains of human and animal origin are closely related to each other and to human ExPEC strains, and that the phylogenetic group of the strains is a major determinant of virulence.
the phylogenetic relationship between avian and ExPEC strains of human origin is very close, but that the zoonotic risk is not established.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the APEC strains of the same phylogenetic group (B2-2) as the ExPEC strains are the most likely to cause disease in chickens and humans.
APEC and human ExPEC are closely related, and the virulence factors that are commonly found in both are not sufficient to explain the host specificity of APEC.
the avian and human E. coli of the same serotype and phylogenetic group share the same set of virulence genes and have similar pathogenic potential.
The main takeaway from our work is that
APEC strains of the same subcluster of phylogenetic groups B2 and D as human ExPEC strains have a similar virulence genotype and are highly virulent for chickens.
the virulence genotype of ExPEC strains is more important than their phylogeny for determining the pathogenic potential of ExPEC strains.
the APEC strains studied belong to a clonal group that is also found in human ExPEC strains, which suggests a possible zoonotic risk.
